newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka Church opposes power plant plan.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka Church opposes power plant plan.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Catholic church said on Wednesday it opposes a planned coal-fired power plant on the island's northwest coast because it would have a negative impact on the lives of the people in the area.
Sri Lanka plans to build a 300-megawatt coal power plant at Kalpitiya, in Puttalam district, some 160 km (100 miles) north of the capital Colombo, to reduce the nation's dependency on hydropower.
The Bishop of Chilaw, who heads the church in Puttalam district, said in a statement that fishing and agriculture in the vicinity would be affected.
The new plant was likely to be a target of Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels and the Sri Lankan navy would probably declare the area around it a high security zone, the statement said.

"There is a real possibility of unexpected attacks on the four-km (2.5 mile) long coal unloading pier, protruding into the sea, thus causing immense damage and disrupting power supply. The whole area will become a security zone," the statement said.
While Sri Lanka is 70 percent Buddhist, the region around the proposed power plant is mainly Christian and the church has a powerful voice.
Plans for the country's first coal-fired plant have run into protests by residents of the area, who say they oppose the project because of fears of environmental pollution and loss of land.
"People also have a genuine fear that tampering with the coast line would lead to erosion of land north of (the coastal village of) Nuraicholai," the bishop said.
Power and Energy Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte said last month that outside interference had prompted people in coastal villages in Kalpitiya to turn against the plans to build the power plant.
In April, one person was killed and several others were wounded when police fired at about 5,000 people demonstrating against the plant.
Ratwatte said a feasibility study for the plant had come to a halt because of opposition.

The Indian Ocean island plans to eventually reduce its reliance on hydropower, which produces up to 85 percent of grid power, to 57 percent after a crippling drought last year forced the government to impose daily eight-hour power cuts.
